guide.title: Thomaston, Connecticut: A Clockmaker's Name on the Naugatuck
guide.intro: Thomaston's land was part of the Farmington proprietors' 1684 purchase of the Mattatuck Plantation, becoming the separate Northbury Parish in 1739, merging into Watertown in 1780, then splitting off again as Plymouth in 1795 — with the section that is now Thomaston known as "Plymouth Hollow." Clockmaking predates the town's namesake: Eli Terry established a factory in 1803 and patented the shelf clock in 1814, but it was Seth Thomas, who came to the hollow to manufacture clocks in 1813, whose name the town took when the legislature confirmed its 1875 separation from Plymouth. Father Michael J. McGivney, founder of the Knights of Columbus, served as pastor of St. Thomas Church here from 1884 until his death in 1890 and was beatified in 2020. After catastrophic 1955 flooding on the Naugatuck River, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built Thomaston Dam, completed in 1960 at a cost of $14 million.

sections.heading: Clockmakers and a catastrophic flood
sections.body: Eli Terry's 1814 shelf-clock patent reduced the cost of a clock from roughly $25 to $5, helping pioneer American mass production, before Seth Thomas built the factory that gave the town its name in 1875. Hurricane Diane dropped record rainfall in August 1955, and the resulting Naugatuck River flood killed dozens statewide and destroyed bridges throughout the valley — Thomaston Dam, completed in 1960 for $14 million, now covers 849 acres of recreation land spanning Thomaston, Harwinton, Litchfield and Plymouth. The Thomaston Opera House, built 1883-1885 by Waterbury architect Robert Hill, doubles uniquely as the town hall and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Route 8, the Naugatuck Valley expressway, runs right through Thomaston along the river with three town exits, and US Route 6 comes in from Bristol and Hartford to the east. There is no passenger rail station in Thomaston — the Naugatuck Railroad tracks through town carry heritage excursion trains and freight between Torrington and a Waterbury interchange, not scheduled passenger transit. The nearest Metro-North service is the Waterbury Branch, terminating in Waterbury to the south — though Branch trains are replaced by buses from July 20, 2026 through May 31, 2027 for station reconstruction.

sections.heading: A heritage railroad and a clock tower
sections.body: The Railroad Museum of New England runs the Naugatuck Railroad out of the 1881 Thomaston Station, marking 30 years of operation in September 2026 with special excursions on restored New Haven equipment. The Seth Thomas Bradstreet House, on Main Street since at least 1838, opens for guided tours on select Saturdays. Black Rock State Park, whose 444 acres border Thomaston, is administered from neighboring Watertown. On Main Street, Black Rock Tavern and Crabby Al's Seafood anchor Thomaston's dining, and the Plume House Inn is the town's one verified bed-and-breakfast.

faq.question: How do I get to Thomaston?
faq.answer: By car — Route 8 runs through town along the Naugatuck River with three local exits, and US Route 6 enters from Bristol and Hartford. There's no passenger rail station in Thomaston; the nearest Metro-North service is the Waterbury Branch, terminating in Waterbury, but Branch trains are replaced by buses from July 20, 2026 through May 31, 2027 for station reconstruction.

faq.question: Why is Thomaston named for a clockmaker?
faq.answer: Seth Thomas came to the village then called Plymouth Hollow in 1813 to manufacture clocks, and by 1856 was labeling them "Thomas Town." On July 6, 1875, the Connecticut legislature confirmed the town's separation from Plymouth under the name Thomaston, in his memory.

faq.question: Can I ride a train at the Railroad Museum of New England?
faq.answer: Yes — the Naugatuck Railroad runs seasonal excursions from the 1881 Thomaston Station, including a "Celebrate 30" weekend in September 2026 marking 30 years of operation, with trains running between Thomaston, Waterville and Thomaston Dam.

faq.question: Is Black Rock State Park in Thomaston?
faq.answer: The park borders Thomaston along the Route 6 corridor, but its official address and administration are in neighboring Watertown. It's a 444-acre park with swimming, hiking and camping around Black Rock Pond.

faq.question: Where can I eat and stay in Thomaston?
faq.answer: Black Rock Tavern and Crabby Al's Seafood anchor Main Street dining, with Clocktown Brewing Company for beer and Cutie Pies for cupcakes and cakes. The Plume House Inn, a restored historic home on Union Street, is Thomaston's one verified bed-and-breakfast.

places.name: Railroad Museum of New England / Naugatuck Railroad — Thomaston Station
places.summary: A Victorian depot built in 1881, damaged by arson in 1993 and stabilized by volunteers since the heritage railroad resumed service in 1996. Seasonal excursions run between Thomaston, Waterville and Thomaston Dam on former New Haven trackage; a "Celebrate 30" weekend runs September 25-27, 2026. Check RMNE's calendar for current excursion dates and pricing.

places.name: Thomaston Opera House (Landmark Community Theatre)
places.summary: Built 1883-1885 by Waterbury architect Robert Hill, a three-story Romanesque brick building with a clock tower, listed on the National Register of Historic Places April 26, 1972 — and uniquely doubling as Thomaston's town hall. Landmark Community Theatre's 2026 season includes Ragtime and The Heart of Rock and Roll.

places.name: Seth Thomas Bradstreet House
places.summary: Standing on Main Street since at least 1838, sold by Seth Thomas to his daughter Amanda Thomas Bradstreet in 1850 and kept in the family for generations before the town acquired it in 2005 with a state grant. Guided tours on the hour, Saturdays in May, June, September and October, free with donations welcome.

places.name: Thomaston Dam
places.summary: Built by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers after catastrophic 1955 Naugatuck River flooding, completed in 1960 at a cost of $14 million; its recreation lands cover 849 acres spanning Thomaston, Harwinton, Litchfield and Plymouth. Hiking, sightseeing, fishing and seasonal snowmobiling on designated trails, open late May through mid-September. Phone (860) 283-5540.

places.name: Thomaston Historical Society Museum
places.summary: Housed atop the Opera House/town hall building, with farm implements, period clothing and Seth Thomas memorabilia including his nightstand and portrait. Visits by appointment only. Phone (860) 283-4421.

places.name: Black Rock Tavern
places.summary: A Main Street tavern serving comfort classics to chef-crafted favorites, near the Opera House, with 10% off for ticket holders. Kitchen Wednesday-Thursday 11:30 a.m.-9 p.m., Friday-Saturday to 10 p.m., Sunday 11 a.m.-8 p.m., closed Monday-Tuesday.

places.name: Clocktown Brewing Company
places.summary: Thomaston's own brewery and taproom with a kitchen, named for the town's clockmaking heritage. Trivia Wednesdays and Jukebox Bingo the first and third Thursday of the month. Hours Wednesday 4-9 p.m., Thursday 4-10 p.m., Friday-Saturday noon-10 p.m., Sunday 11 a.m.-8 p.m.

places.name: Crabby Al's Seafood
places.summary: A seafood-and-American-classics house near the railroad station, with a seasonal outdoor deck, raw bar, Sunday brunch and live bands Friday and Saturday. Kitchen Sunday-Thursday 11 a.m.-10 p.m., Friday-Saturday to 11 p.m.

places.name: Rozzi's Restaurant
places.summary: A local American diner serving breakfast all day, lunch and dinner, with a drive-thru window, delivery and a Breakfast Club loyalty program. Hours Monday-Thursday 7 a.m.-8 p.m., Friday-Saturday to 9 p.m., Sunday 7 a.m.-3 p.m.

places.name: Cutie Pies Bakery & Café
places.summary: A small Main Street boutique bakery that opened in 2023, specializing in cupcakes, cakes and custom sweets for showers and birthdays. Hours not posted online — call (860) 484-4838.

places.name: Plume House Inn
places.summary: A restored historic home run as a bed and breakfast, with rooms furnished to the period of the house, scratch-made breakfasts from garden produce and backyard honey, and a "Hunter Library" sitting room. Named a Best of Connecticut honoree by CT Insider. Phone (860) 480-2490.
